To define $ \Delta S_{conf} $ we begin by comparing the adsorption of alkanes in five different zeolite structures: MFI, CHA, TON, FAU, and MOR. Depicted in Figure 2A is the relationship between the entropy of an adsorbed molecule (alkanes and permanent gases) and its gas-phase entropy, where the molecular entropy on the surface never exceeds that in the gas phase. While a significant loss in entropy occurs in all five zeolites, the absolute loss in entropy is distinct for each framework. Adsorbates in TON exhibit the largest loss in entropy upon adsorption, while FAU results in the smallest entropic losses. ABSTRACT: Confinement of hydrocarbons in nanoscale pockets and pores provides tunable capability for controlling molecules in catalysts, sorbents, and membranes for reaction and separation applications. While computation of the enthalpic interactions of hydrocarbons in confined spaces has improved, understanding and predicting the entropy of confined molecules remains a challenge. Here we show, using a set of nine aluminosilicate zeolite frameworks with broad variation in pore and cavity structure, that the entropy of adsorption can be predicted as a linear combination of rotational and translational entropy. The extent of entropy lost upon adsorption is predicted using only a single material descriptor, the occupiable volume ( $ V_{occ} $). Predictive capability of confined molecular entropy permits an understanding of the relation with adsorption enthalpy, the ability to computationally screen microporous materials, and an understanding of the role of confinement on the kinetics of molecules in confined spaces.

On the basis of this shape-selective feature , highly effective molecular separations and selective catalytic conversions can be achieved within zeolitic structures that are difficult to accomplish with other materials and/or techniques . $ ^ { 1-3 } $ So far, several shape-selectivity mechanisms have been elucidated and applications identified. $ ^{2-18} $ In common molecular sieving, bulky molecules adsorb preferentially over bulkier species as a result of steric constraints imposed by the zeolites' framework, e.g., linear alkane molecules compared to branched isomers. $ ^{19-23} $ Besides this common adsorption competition based on molecular bulkiness, the reverse phenomenon can also occur, i.e., competitive adsorption in favor of the bulkier species. Experiments revealed preferential adsorption of branched alkanes over their linear isomers on specific zeolites with tubular pore systems such as SAPO-5 and Mordenite. $ ^{24-28} $ Molecular simulations indicated that in such zeolites, depending on conditions, branched alkanes are preferentially adsorbed at the expense of linear isomers. $ ^{29-34} $ The present manuscript discusses the mechanisms of shape selectivity in n- and isoalkane adsorption on zeolite MCM-22. This zeolite with IZA code MWW is a relatively new synthetic material that has an unusual and quite complex pore structure. $ ^{35} $ Its framework is composed of two independent pore systems. The enthalpy and the entropy contributions to the Gibbs free energies were calculated at T = 298 K and partial pressure of 1 atm (101325 Pa). The enthalpy (H) of gas-phase pyridine and acetonitrile molecules is defined as the sum of total electronic energy ( $ E_{el} $), internal vibrational energy ( $ E_{v} $), zero-point vibrational energy (ZPVE), as well as the rotational and translational contributions to the internal energy: $ H = E_{el} + E_{v} + ZPVE + E_{R} + E_{t} $. The corresponding calculated entropies (S) includes translational, ( $ S_{t} $) vibrational, ( $ S_{v} $) and rotational ( $ S_{r} $) degrees of freedom: $ S = S_{t} + S_{v} + S_{r} $. All the considered systems are in singlet state, thus the electronic contribution to the entropy is zero. Since both adsorbed molecules are constrained in the zeolite cavity their entropy contributions in the adsorption complexes were corrected as follows: the translational and rotational degrees of freedom were reduced by 1 and 1.28 [37]. The Gibbs free energies of the zeolite support consist of only vibrational and electronic contributions. The expressions of all enthalpy and entropy contributions can be found in Ref. [38].

The first attempts to describe guest-induced flexibility in zeolites were done using molecular dynamics simulations. $ ^{79-82} $ Rigid zeolitic force fields were dynamically modified using transition state theory to include lattice flexibility, and the results obtained by these models were in good agreement with experimental data. $ ^{79-81,83,84} $ It was shown that framework flexibility in silicalite-1 (MFI-type framework) is responsible for the adsorption of large molecules such as isobutane and heptane with inflection behavior at high loadings, $ ^{80} $ while enhanced self-diffusivity at low loadings of short alkanes (i.e. methane and n-butane) was observed. $ ^{81} $ Framework flexibility is also crucial for aromatics adsorption on MFI zeolite, especially at high pressures. $ ^{84,85} $ While the use of rigid zeolitic models led to the underestimation of the aromatics adsorption in MFI zeolite by a factor of two, $ ^{84,85} $ the use of flexible models to simulate diffusion coefficients of various alkanes in silicalite-1 zeolite resulted in a convergence of experimental and theoretical values. $ ^{86} $ Recently by using in situ integrated differential phase contrast scanning transmission electron microscopy (iDPC-STEM) while adsorbing benzene molecules on MFI zeolite, Xiong et al. showed that the MFI structure goes through severe deformations giving another proof of guest-induced flexibility in zeolites (see Fig. 4). $ ^{87} $

2.4.4. Trapdoor. Traditional diﬀusion models primarily consider two types of interactions: those between guest molecules (guest–guest) and those between guest molecules and the zeolite framework (guest–host). However, when cations are present in the zeolite structure, a third interaction—involving guest molecules, the framework, and cations (guest–host-cation)—must also be accounted for. A striking example of such ternary interactions is the well-known ‘‘molecular trapdoor’’. This phenomenon, also referred to as the ‘‘gating effect’’, describes a unique molecular sieving mechanism in certain zeolites and related porous materi- als. Here, extra-framework cations function as dynamic gate- keepers at pore apertures, selectively controlling molecular diffusion to achieve highly discriminative adsorption and separation.9,147,187 To date, ‘‘trapdoor’’ has been observed in several zeolites, including RHO (DNL-6),188–190 CHA (SAPO-34, SSZ-13),147,191,192 MWF (ZSM-25),149,193 HEU (Clinoptilolite),194

The turnover rates of olefin formation during cyclohexanol (CyOH) dehydration within the autoclave reactor initially increase with the local ionic strength within a micropore, and further decrease along ionic strength promotion, shown as a volcano-shaped dependence of TOFs on the ionic strength of zeolites. But the formation and size of the H₃O⁺(H₂O)ₙ₋₁ in the zeolite pores limit the adsorption of CyOH, e.g., size exclusion effects, and decrease reaction rates. In the following appendix , we derive the entropy of adsorption in the case of infinite dilution and show how it may be related to familiar thermodynamic quantities ( cf . eq 5 ) . To begin , we define our adsorption entropy in the limit of infinite dilution via

$$ \Delta s_{\mathrm{ads}}^{\infty}=\lim_{N/V\rightarrow0}\left[\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial N}\right)_{V,T,\mathrm{ads}}-\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial N}\right)_{V,T,\mathrm{gas}}\right] $$

$$ =S_{ads}(N=1,V,T)-S_{gas}(N=1,V,T) $$

where the subscripts “ads” and “gas” labels identify the adsorbed (confined) and gas (bulk) phases, respectively. Given the constraints of a fixed number of molecules (N), volume (V), and temperature (T), it is natural to continue working in the canonical ensemble. (As in the main text, lowercase symbols identify intensive molecular or molar properties, whereas the uppercase indicates an extensive property.) For the molecules that we examine in this work (e.g., rigid molecules with no internal degrees of freedom), the canonical partition function Q may be expressed as

$$ \begin{aligned}Q(N,V,T)&=Q_{trans}(N,V,T)Q_{rot}(N,V,T)\\&\quad\times Z(N,V,T)\end{aligned} $$

where $ Q_{trans} $ and $ Q_{rot} $ are the translational and rotational partition functions (which are unaffected by confinement) and Z is the configurational partition function. The translational and rotational partition functions are available in the usual statistical mechanics texts $ ^{44,45} $ but are ultimately unimportant for the derivation that follows.

descriptor_candidates.name: conf_vol_ratio_entropy_loss
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Hypothesis (inference): entropy loss fraction (s_gas - s_ads)/R grows logarithmically with the mismatch between the occupiable accessible volume per gram (AV) and the geometric molecular-scale confinement length (cube root of molecular volume divided by framework density on its native scale). Formulas re-express the fixed 14 inputs only; improved MAE alone is not a discovery claim.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Mechanism (inference from E01, E02): confinement reduces translational/rotational freedom; the fraction of gas-phase entropy retained depends on the ratio of free volume accessible to the molecule relative to its own size. Occupiable volume was shown to be a single predictive descriptor for confined entropy (E02); here it is combined with a molecular-size scale (Vol/density cube root) to form a confinement-mismatch term.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Falsified if including this descriptor in the neural network does not reduce MAE of entropy loss/R relative to the same network trained without it, across multiple random splits, or if the sign of its effect on entropy loss is inconsistent (negative correlation with loss) in cross-validation.

descriptor_candidates.name: shape_anisotropy_confinement
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Hypothesis (inference): entropy loss increases with molecular shape anisotropy (ratio of largest to smallest principal moment of inertia) when the pore-limiting diameter (lsd_p) is close to the molecule's smallest dimension (PBF); elongated molecules in tight tubular pores lose more rotational entropy than compact molecules of equal volume. Source evidence only establishes that confinement reduces entropy and that pore topology matters (E01, E04); the specific anisotropy-pore-size interaction is inference.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Mechanism: in channels narrower than the molecular cross-section allows free rotation, rotational degrees of freedom freeze out; the number of rotational modes lost depends on molecular anisotropy (PMI ratio) and the ratio of pore diameter to molecular thickness. TON-type tubular pores show largest entropy loss for linear alkanes (E01), consistent with anisotropy-controlled rotational constraint (E04 shape selectivity).
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Falsified if the interaction term contributes no reduction in MAE of entropy loss/R versus the full 14-input baseline network, or if the fitted partial dependence of entropy loss on the anisotropy term is flat or sign-reversed for molecules confined in tubular vs. cage frameworks.

descriptor_candidates.name: surface_area_damping
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Hypothesis (inference): entropy loss is damped when the framework offers large accessible surface area per unit molecular contact area (ASA relative to LabuteASA), because adsorption on extended flat surfaces retains more rotational/translational freedom than confinement in small pockets; the largest free-sphere diameter (lsd_f) modulates how much of the surface is effectively usable. Established literature relations used: volume-controlled confinement entropy (E02, known_relation) and pore-size control (E01); the surface-area damping formulation is a new combination (uncertain).
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Mechanism: adsorption entropy loss is smallest in large-cage frameworks (FAU, E01), where accessible surface area per molecule is greatest. A large ratio of framework surface area to molecular surface area means the molecule can translate/rotate over extended surfaces rather than being pinned, reducing entropy loss; sqrt(lsd_f) scales this with the largest cavity dimension.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Falsified if this descriptor's partial dependence on entropy loss/R is not monotonically decreasing with ASA/(LabuteASA) in the trained network, or if adding it to the 14-input baseline yields no statistically significant MAE improvement (e.g., overlapping error bars over repeated cross-validation).

descriptor_candidates.name: pore_mismatch_packing
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Hypothesis (inference): entropy loss fraction (s_gas - s_ads)/R increases when the cube root of occupiable volume per gram is small relative to the pore-limiting diameter AND the molecular volume (Vol) is large relative to the surface-contact scale (ASA times largest free diameter). This captures a two-part mechanism: tight pores restrict translation, while bulky molecules touching extended framework walls lose configurational (positional) entropy through dense packing constraints. Evidence E01 and E02 establish only that confinement reduces entropy and that occupiable volume alone predicts entropy loss; the packing/contact-scale interaction is inference.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Mechanism (inference): translational entropy loss is governed by free-length scales (Vocc^(1/3) vs pore-limiting diameter, E02, E01 known_relation), while positional/configurational entropy loss grows when a molecule's volume is large compared to the surface area it can contact at the framework's largest cavity dimension. Combining both scales in one log-additive descriptor tests whether translational and packing constraints contribute independently to entropy loss.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Falsified if adding this descriptor to the 14-input neural network does not reduce MAE of entropy loss/R versus the retained baseline (conf_vol_ratio_entropy_loss network) across repeated random splits, or if the partial dependence on either log term is flat or sign-reversed in cross-validation.

descriptor_candidates.name: anisotropy_aperture_freezeout
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Hypothesis (inference): rotational entropy freeze-out is governed by how many rotational axes are constrained, approximated by the ratio of the intermediate to smallest principal moment (PMI2/PMI1), scaled by the mismatch between the molecule's geometric span (cube root of Vol, SPAN, GeDi) and the pore aperture (lsd_p) and its thinnest dimension (PBF). Round-1 candidate shape_anisotropy_confinement used only PMI3/minimum(PMI1,PMI2); here the intermediate-axis ratio is proposed as the better proxy for which rotational modes freeze out in near-cylindrical channels. The anisotropy-aperture mechanism is inference; E01 and E04 only establish framework-dependent loss and shape selectivity.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Mechanism (inference): a molecule in a channel retains rotation about the channel axis but loses the two orthogonal rotations; which axis survives depends on molecular anisotropy. The intermediate/smallest moment ratio distinguishes rod-like from plate-like constraint, while the SPAN/GeDi terms encode the molecular dimension distribution relative to the aperture (lsd_p) and minimum thickness (PBF), testing whether multi-dimensional size matching outperforms the single PMI-ratio form that failed in round 1.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Falsified if this descriptor yields no MAE improvement over the retained baseline, or if its marginal contribution is statistically indistinguishable from the rejected round-1 anisotropy descriptor (i.e., the intermediate-axis formulation adds nothing), assessed over repeated cross-validation splits.

descriptor_candidates.name: flexibility_window_strain
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Hypothesis (inference): entropy loss is largest in frameworks with a large window-to-cavity aspect ratio (lsd_f/lsd_p) when the molecular volume is close to the occupiable volume per framework density (mismatch near 1), because such size-matched molecules are locked at window junctions where cage-to-cage hopping is required; frameworks with low framework-density-per-accessible-volume (more open, flexible lattices, E06) partially compensate by allowing guest-induced deformation. E10 establishes that framework distortion and molecular contraction occur near size mismatch; the quantitative lock-in descriptor is inference.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Mechanism (inference): when a molecule's size nearly equals the occupiable volume scale, it cannot translate freely within a cage and must wait at windows, freezing configurational entropy; a large lsd_f/lsd_p ratio indicates cages connected by narrow windows (cage-like frameworks like CHA show larger losses than channel frameworks, E01). The exp(-density/(AV)) term tests whether open, low-density frameworks damp this penalty, consistent with guest-induced framework flexibility (E06) and lattice distortion near mismatch (E10).
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Falsified if the descriptor does not reduce MAE of entropy loss/R relative to the retained baseline network across repeated splits, or if the partial dependence shows that the lock-in penalty (mismatch near 1 combined with large lsd_f/lsd_p) does not correlate with larger entropy loss in cage-type versus channel-type frameworks in cross-validation.

descriptor_candidates.name: moment_surface_match
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Hypothesis (inference): entropy loss fraction (s_gas - s_ads)/R grows with the ratio of the molecular's longest inertial dimension (cube root of the largest principal moment, PMI3) to the pore-limiting diameter (lsd_p), but is damped when the framework offers high molecular-level surface area per unit accessible volume (LabuteASA/AV), because extended contact surfaces let long molecules lie flat and retain one translational and one rotational degree of freedom. Round-1 and round-2 anisotropy descriptors failed using pure PMI ratios without a surface-damping channel; this tests whether surface availability, not anisotropy alone, controls rotational freeze-out of elongated molecules.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Mechanism (inference): translational and rotational modes freeze out when molecular length exceeds the aperture (E01: TON tubular pores show largest loss), but a molecule adsorbed on an extended surface retains 2D translation and rotation about the surface normal, so the entropy penalty should scale with length mismatch times surface scarcity. E01/E04 establish only framework-dependent loss and shape selectivity; the surface-damping interaction is a new, testable inference.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Falsified if adding this descriptor to the 14-input network does not reduce MAE of entropy loss/R below the retained baseline (0.5501 R) across repeated random splits, or if partial dependence on the surface-ratio factor is flat or positive (anti-damping) in cross-validation.

descriptor_candidates.name: density_weighted_packing_limit
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Hypothesis (inference): entropy loss is largest when (i) molecular volume approaches the geometric pore volume per framework-density unit (Vol/(AV*density) near unity, dense packing) and (ii) the cavity-window contrast (lsd_f - lsd_p) is small relative to the molecule's geometric dimension spread (GeDi), meaning the molecule cannot find size refuge in cavities and is constrained everywhere. Unlike round-2's flexibility_window_strain (which used an absolute mismatch term and failed), this form predicts the opposite regime: tight, homogeneous confinement (small cavity-window contrast) rather than window lock-in drives loss.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Mechanism (inference): configurational entropy of a confined molecule scales with the positional phase-space volume; when the molecule nearly fills the pore everywhere (Vol ~ pore volume, lsd_f ~ lsd_p), positional freedom collapses uniformly. E02 establishes occupiable volume as a single predictive descriptor (known_relation); the homogeneous-vs-heterogeneous confinement contrast via lsd_f/lsd_p/GeDi is a new competing hypothesis to the window lock-in mechanism rejected in round 2.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Falsified if this descriptor does not beat the retained baseline MAE across repeated splits, or if its fitted partial dependence shows entropy loss increasing (rather than decreasing) with the exp(-(lsd_f - lsd_p)/(GeDi)) factor, contradicting the homogeneous-confinement mechanism.

descriptor_candidates.name: aspect_pocket_compression
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Hypothesis (inference): entropy loss fraction grows with the ratio of molecular length (SPAN) to pore-limiting diameter (lsd_p) — the 'rod-in-tube' compression — scaled by the framework's surface-per-mass availability (ASA relative to a density-weighted molecular volume scale) and reduced by how small the molecule's thinnest dimension (PBF) is compared to the largest cavity (lsd_f): flat/thin molecules in large cages can orient to preserve rotational entropy. This replaces round-1's failed PMI-ratio and sqrt(lsd_f) log-area forms with a direct dimensional-mismatch product using SPAN and PBF instead of inertial moments.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Mechanism (inference): statistical mechanics of confined partition functions (E09) implies the configurational integral shrinks when molecular dimensions exceed pore dimensions; the surviving rotational modes depend on whether the molecule's minimal cross-section fits (PBF vs lsd_f). E01/E02 establish confinement and occupiable-volume control (known_relation); the SPAN/lsd_p compression with PBF/lsd_f orientation escape is a new dimensional formulation that round-1 candidates did not test.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Falsified if including this descriptor yields no MAE reduction versus the retained baseline over repeated cross-validation, or if the partial dependence on SPAN/lsd_p is non-monotonic with sign inconsistent with monotonically increasing loss for rods in tight tubes.

retained.name: conf_vol_ratio_entropy_loss
retained.hypothesis: Hypothesis (inference): entropy loss fraction (s_gas - s_ads)/R grows logarithmically with the mismatch between the occupiable accessible volume per gram (AV) and the geometric molecular-scale confinement length (cube root of molecular volume divided by framework density on its native scale). Formulas re-express the fixed 14 inputs only; improved MAE alone is not a discovery claim.
